connection: The Skomer vole is a subspecies of bank vole endemic to the island of Skomer, off the west coast of Wales. It is found nowhere else, and the island population is thought to descend from bank voles that people brought there after the last glaciation.

The Manx shearwater nests in burrows on small islands, and three-quarters of the British and Irish birds breed on just three islands: Skomer, Skokholm and Rùm. Skomer and Skokholm are therefore principal strongholds for the species.
Skokholm is home to a major part of Europe's population of European storm petrels. The island has been the site of the most thorough British studies of this seabird.
The northern gannet nests in a small number of very large colonies, and Grassholm in Wales is one of the largest. The island is a principal stronghold for this North Atlantic seabird.
Ramsey Island has the most important grey seal breeding colony in southern Britain. Grey seals breed on the island, and that colony is the most important in the south of Britain.
Ramsey Island is one of the best sites in Wales for choughs. The birds are attracted to the island by an ample supply of dung beetles.

Experts on British apples judged an old tree on Bardsey Island to be the only example of a previously unrecorded cultivar, the Bardsey apple. The tree is believed to be the survivor of an orchard once tended by monks on the island, and the cultivar is named for Bardsey.

Lundy cabbage is a primitive brassica endemic to the island of Lundy, off the southwestern coast of England. It grows wild nowhere else in the world, and its isolation on Lundy has produced a species of its own, along with beetles that feed only on it.
The Lundy cabbage flea beetle is a flea beetle endemic to the island of Lundy, where it lives and feeds upon the endemic Lundy cabbage. It is known from nowhere else in the world.

The Glanville fritillary is a checkerspot butterfly that, in the United Kingdom, is highly restricted and confined to the Isle of Wight. Even on that island it is largely limited to the southern coast, so the Isle of Wight is its British stronghold.

Wood calamint is a mint-family herb that, in Britain, is limited to a single site on the Isle of Wight. It grows there in ancient deciduous woodland on chalk, and that island holds the species' only British population.

The lesser white-toothed shrew on the Isles of Scilly is known as the Scilly shrew, and that population is isolated from the species' wider range. It is unusual there in living on the islands' beaches, where it feeds almost exclusively on amphipods.

source_title: List of endemic species of the British Isles
connection: The Scilly bee, Bombus muscorum scyllonius, is an endemic bumblebee of the Isles of Scilly and is currently known only from St Agnes, Great Ganilly and Great Arthur. It was formerly found on the archipelago's other inhabited islands except Bryher.

The least adder's-tongue is a tiny fern whose British distribution is restricted to one small area of coastal heath on St Agnes in the Isles of Scilly. That island is the species' only British locality, so it is the national stronghold.
The wild peony was introduced to Steep Holm, possibly by monks, and has also naturalised on nearby Flat Holm. Those two islands are the only known places in the UK where the species grows wild.

Wild leek is one of the rare plants of Flat Holm, and the island is one of only five places in the UK where it is found. The leek's presence is part of why the island's maritime grassland is protected.

Brownsea Island in Poole Harbour is populated exclusively by red squirrels rather than grey squirrels. The island is one of the English refuges where the native red squirrel persists after a drastic decline elsewhere in Britain.

This Mediterranean door snail, sometimes called the Cliveden snail in Britain, was recorded from Brownsea Castle on Brownsea Island. It lives there on stonework and statuary imported from Italy, an accidental introduction that has remained established on the island.

Red squirrels were taken to Tresco in the Isles of Scilly and released there, although the species is not indigenous to those islands. Tresco was chosen as a safe haven because it has no grey squirrels and no foxes.

After non-native grey squirrels were removed, the remnant red squirrel population on Anglesey recovered. The island now has the largest red squirrel population in Wales and is the species' main Welsh refuge.

Havergate Island is known for its pied avocets and holds the UK's largest breeding population of the species. The birds were found breeding on the island in the 1940s after they had been lost as a British breeding bird, and the island has been managed for them since.

The roseate tern is one of the UK's rarest breeding seabirds, and the country's most important colony is on Coquet Island, Northumberland. Coquet Island is the principal British stronghold for this scarce tern.

Annet is of outstanding importance as a seabird colony, and the European storm petrel has a nationally important breeding population there. The only breeding sites for this petrel in England are in the Isles of Scilly, and Annet holds the majority of them.

A particularly famous colony of common eiders lives on the Farne Islands in Northumberland. The ducks are still often called St Cuthbert's ducks or Cuddy's ducks there, after the saint associated with the islands' birds.

The Lindisfarne helleborine is an orchid discovered on Lindisfarne, also called Holy Island. The plants were formerly identified as dune helleborine, but they were found to be genetically distinct and were given the scientific name Epipactis sancta.
